message.content:
**Short‑answer:** A fully‑equipped crew of skilled painters could lay down a new coat of paint on the Eiffel Tower in **about six to eight weeks** (roughly 40–50 workdays). If you’re doing it “by hand” without heavy‑lift rigs, scaffolding, or spray‑painting machines, expect somewhere between **three and nine months**, depending largely on how many people you can deploy simultaneously and whether you’re allowed to keep the tower open to tourists during the job. --- ### Why those numbers? | Factor | Typical value / assumption | |--------|----------------------------| | **Total exterior surface** | ≈ 25 000 m² (≈ 270 000 ft²) – this includes the visible faces of the latticework, balconies, staircases, elevators, and the roof.
*(Sources: engineering studies & historical renovation records.)* | | **Paint application method** | • Spray guns + high‑pressure hoses (industrial standard)
• Hand‑held brushes/scrapers for tight spots
*Spray gives ~250 sq ft/hr per gun.* | | **Crew size** | 10–15 experienced painters + 2 supervisors + rigging support → 13–17 people.
With larger crews (e.g., 30–35 people) you cut time proportionally. | | **Work hours** | Standard shift: 8 h/day, 5 d/wk. Night shifts add extra capacity but increase safety costs. | | **Productivity** | Average productive output per painter: 150–180 sq ft/h after accounting for setup, travel between platforms, breaks, and re‑coating of already-painted panels. | #### Calculation (typical scenario) ``` Surface area : 270,000 ft² Painter output : 170 ft²/h × 8 h/d = 1,360 ft²/d per person Number of painters : 14 Daily coverage : 19,040 ft²/d Days needed : 270,000 ÷ 19,040 ≈ 14.2 d Add prep/cleanup : + 3–4 d Result : ~18–22 calendar days ``` Because the tower isn’t a flat wall—you have to climb, move ladders, secure scaffolds, and sometimes wait for wind conditions—the real‑world pace slows down. Adding a buffer for weather, logistics, and tourist traffic brings us to the **six‑to‑eight week window** quoted above. --- ### Historical context - **Every 7–10 years** the tower receives a fresh coat of paint as part of its routine maintenance program. Those intervals reflect both the natural corrosion cycle of wrought iron and the practicalities of scheduling such a massive project. - Past refurbishments (e.g., 1999–2000, 2013–2014) involved teams of dozens of specialists and lasted **approximately three months** overall, though some phases overlapped with visitor operations. - When the tower was first built (1887), the original paint job took **over a year** because labor was manual and technology limited. So, if you’re planning a hypothetical repaint today: | Scenario | Timeframe | Notes | |----------|-----------|-------| | **Professional crew, spray‑gun tech, minimal downtime** | 6–8 weeks | Fastest feasible route. | | **Large volunteer effort, mixed methods** | 3–4 months | More flexible but slower. | | **Historic preservation style, meticulous hand‑painted detail** | 6+ months | Highest quality, lowest speed. | | **Full closure of tower for safety** | 9–12 months | Allows uninterrupted work but disrupts tourism revenue. | --- ### Bottom line Assuming you hire a competent contractor who can bring in enough manpower, equipment, and permits, you’ll likely see the Eiffel Tower finished within **two months**. If you want to preserve the daily flow of millions of visitors—or if budget constraints limit your crew size—it could stretch out to **four to five months**. Either way, the iconic landmark won’t stay bare for very long!
